explanation: Delayed-type hypersensitivity skin testing is a convenient and cost- effective method for assessing cell-mediated immune responses to a variety of antigens. The PPD reagent is comprised of antigens purified from Mycobacteria and these antigens are taken up by dermal macrophages after injection into the dermis. When these stimulated macrophages migrate into the draining lymph node, they encounter memory T lymphocytes from the prior primary infection. The memory T lymphocytes are reactivated and recirculate back to the injection site, where they further interact with antigens from the PPD reagent and macrophages. explanation: The vignette alludes to the diagnosis of Blau syndrome, a rare systemic granulomatosis that presents in childhood with a classic triad of dermatitis, arthritis, and uveitis. There are both familial (autosomal dominant inheritance) and sporadic forms of the disease with the causative gene having been identified as NOD2. Patients often present in the first year of life with dermatitis as the initial finding. The dermatitis manifests as a fine and scaly papular erythematous eruption that may remit and recur (see image below). It may develop into a markedly scaly rash in later stages, and each focus of inflammation may heal with a scar. Second to present is an arthritis that affects multiple joints (polyarthritis). There is a predilection for the distal joints, particularly the knees, ankles, wrists, and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints. The axial skeleton is not affected. Chronic polyarthritis may unfortunately lead to joint deformation. Uveitis often presents after the dermatitis and arthritis. The uveitis is nearly always bilateral, granulomatous, and though initially anterior in location, frequently extends posteriorly into a panuveitis. Posterior disease most commonly takes the form of a multifocal choroiditis. The typical sequelae of chronic ocular inflammation, such as synechiae, cataracts, and band keratopathy often occur. Aside from the classic triad, the manifestations of Blau syndrome are protean and may include: vasculitis, nephritis, pericarditis, pneumonitis (leading to interstitial lung disease), among others. Treatment of Blau syndrome rests in immunomodulatory therapy though there is no consensus regarding the optimal treatment regimen. Tumor necrosis factor (TF) inhibitor shows some promise in efficacy. Due to its rarity, there is a great deal of variation in treatment regimens and long-term data on this unfortunately debilitating disorder are needed. The other answer choices allude to other panuveitides. Hilar pulmonary nodules (Answer A) and infiltration of the lacrimal gland are typical of sarcoidosis, and oral aphthous ulcers (Answer D) are typical of Behcet's disease. Of note, when Blau disease was first discovered, some considered it to be an early form of sarcoidosis (indeed, "Early Onset Sarcoidosis" was a term used to describe the sporadic form of the disease). Though this is not strictly correct, there certainly are similarities between the two conditions in terms of symptomatology. question: In a patient with no known drug allergies, what is the recommended systemic antibiotic for the treatment of ocular syphilis?
explanation: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommend parenteral penicillin G as the the preferred treatment of choice for all stages of syphilis. In patients with penicillin allergy, several therapeutic options have been reported to be effective in treating syphilis, including treatment with tetracycline, doxycycline, chloramphenicol, and ceftriaxone. However, no antibiotic, other than penicillin, has been found to be effective in consistently and effectively treating neurosyphilis, congenital syphilis, or infection in pregnant patients or patients with HIV. Therefore, these patients who also have penicillin-allergy, penicillin desensitization and treatment with penicillin is highly recommended. Acquired syphilis with ocular involvement should be treated as neurosyphilis, so a lumbar puncture with examination of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is warranted for all cases of ocular syphilis. Regardless of CSF results, antibiotic treatment for ocular syphilis requires neurologic dosing regimens. Currently, the CDC recommends two possible regimens for the treatment of neurosyphilis: 1. 18 to 24 million units (MU) of intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G daily for 10-14 days. 2. (If compliance with therapy can be ensured) 2.4 MU/day of intramuscular procaine penicillin plus probenecid 500 mg 4 times a day for 10-14 days. Side Note: probenecid is a medication that is traditionally used in the treatment of gout, which is a form of arthritis caused by a build up of uric acid in the joints. Probenecid acts on renal tubular cells by competitively inhibiting the reabsorption of urate at the proximal convoluted tubule, increasing the urinary excretion of uric acid and decreasing serum urate levels. At the proximal and distal tubules, probenecid competitively inhibits the secretion of many weak organic acids, including penicillin. This results in an increased plasma concentration and extended half-life of penicillin. After completion of either of these treatment regimens, further treatment with intramuscular benzathine penicillin G, 2.4 MU weekly for three weeks may be administered if a longer duration of therapy is preferred by the clinician. Syphilis is caused by the spirochete Treponema Pallidum, which replicates once every 30 hours. Many clinicians believe higher rates of treatment failure may occur with sole treatment with intramuscular penicillin, because it may not achieve adequate and sustained intraocular levels required to achieve an adequate bactericidal effect. Therefore, most clinicians recommend initially treating neurosyphilis with intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G, 18 to 24 million units (MU) daily for 10-14 days, followed by intramuscular benzathine penicillin G, 2.4 MU weekly for three weeks. explanation: Onchocerciasias is caused by the filarial nematode Onchocerca volvulus. Onchocerca volvulus has a multiple stage life cycle. Humans are the only definitive host. A definitive host or primary host is a host in which the parasite reaches maturity and, if possible, reproduces sexually. The blackfly (genus Simulium) acts as an obligate intermediate host. Human infection occurs when a blackfly bites a human host and introduces Onchocerca volvulus microfilariae (larvae) into the human host. The microfilariae develop into macrofilariae (adult worms) and mate in the subcutaneous tissues of the human host. During adulthood, the female worm can shed hundreds of thousands of microfilariae that can migrate throughout the body of the human host (particularly to the skin and the eye). The Onchocerca volvulus lifecycle continues when a human host is bitten by the blackfly and ingests microfilariae. Once inside the blackfly, the microfilariae penetrate the gut of the fly and migrate to the thoracic flight muscles, where they further develop along the larval stages and then migrate back to the head and the proboscis (feeding/sucking appendage) of the blackfly. However, FUS is a diagnosis of exclusion and typically other infectious etiologies such as tuberculosis and syphilis should be excluded. explanation: Corticosteroid-induced ocular hypertension is an open angle glaucoma cause by prolonged use of topical, periocular, intravitreal, inhaled, or systemic corticosteroids. One third of the population may experience an increase in IOP in response to the local or svstemic use of corticosteroids, but the response varies among individuals. Steroid- induced ocular hypertension presents with an open anterior chamber angle, and the rise in OP appears to be due to outflow reduction. The time frame when steroid induced ocular hypertension occurs depends on the specific drug, the dosage, the frequency, the rout of a administration and the susceptibility of the individual patient. Although the majority of studies report that IOP usually rises 3-6 weeks after the beginning of topical steroid use, some elevation in IOP can be found as early as the first or second week. Most patients with elevated IOP in steroid-response glaucoma experience a return to pretreatment IOP levels within 10 days to 3 weeks after the discontinuation of steroid therapy. explanation: Cyclodestructive procedures (e.g. diode cyclophotocoagulation) generally should be avoided since they induce a tremendous amount of additional inflammation which may lead to chronic hypotony and eventual phthisis bulbi. In many clinical centers, a tube shunt procedure (e.g. Ahmed valve) is the procedure of choice for uveitic glaucoma patients since filtering surgery often fails quickly in the presence of chronic inflammation. And yes, a trabeculectomy (or ExPRESS shunt, etc) is at high risk for failure in uveitic glaucoma patients.
